title: Discord 的 IPO 之路需要游戏开发者
content:
Discord’s Path to IPO Needs Game Developers
Skip to content
Weekly Digest
Discord’s Path to IPO Needs Game Developers
By Naavik •   November 15, 2026
Source:
Discord
In January, Discord
confidentially filed for an IPO
, making it the most important gaming-related listing since Roblox. The company heading toward its public-market debut looks quite different from the one that last raised money in 2021 at a $15B valuation: co-founder Jason Citron stepped down as CEO last year and was replaced by Humam Sakhnini, a former vice chairman of Activision Blizzard, while its new chief business officer, Jules Shumaker,
led advertising at EA, Zynga, and Unity
.
That reshaped leadership team reflects a shift in who Discord thinks its customer is and where the growth to propel it through IPO will come from. For most of its history, Discord focused on serving and monetizing gamers themselves, primarily through Nitro subscriptions. Now, as
CTO Stan Vishnevskiy recently put it
, the company has “made developers into a second primary customer” through ads, game commerce, and a social SDK. Discord has courted game developers as customers to varying degrees in the past; what is different this time, and what does it mean for Discord as a public company?
Discord’s User Base: The Product to Sell to Game Developers
Discord reports
more than 90M daily active users
, with over 90% playing games. But the composition of that gaming audience matters as much as its size. Among the
100 largest public servers
on the platform, 38 are dedicated to Roblox games, accounting for 35% of the total audience across the top 100. The Steal a Brainrot server (7.4M members) is nearly twice the size of Marvel Rivals (4.1M) and considerably larger than Valorant (3.0M). Most of the remaining top 100 servers are PC and console titles, with a notable cluster from Chinese publishers operating games in international markets. NetEase, HoYoverse, Kuro, and Tencent all run servers in the top 100.
Approximately 20% of the combined audience across the top 500 servers belongs to communities that are not directly gaming-related. This includes social hangouts, AI tools (Midjourney was widely used through Discord in 2022–23), and communities centered on popular IPs and streamers. Many of these “non-gaming” categories significantly overlap with gaming, echoing Discord’s own statement that 90% of its users play games.
Top 500 Discord Servers by Category | Source:
Discord
, Naavik
It’s worth noting that public servers are only a slice of Discord’s overall activity, as much of it takes place in small, private friend groups. These membership counts are also cumulative, not measures of active users. Still, the picture is clear enough: Discord’s audience is young and highly engaged, with a strong concentration around Roblox and live-service PC and console games. Beyond gaming, it also serves as a community platform resembling a communication service like WhatsApp. That audience is the constant in Discord’s story. What is changing is how Discord monetizes it.
A Decade of Monetizing Gamers
Discord’s monetization story began with the Nitro subscription. Launched nearly a decade ago, the
$9.99-per-month
plan (with a $2.99 Basic tier) offers a combination of status and utility: larger file uploads, higher-quality video streaming, custom emoji usable across servers, profile customization, and “boosts” that upgrade a favorite server. According to Discord’s SVP of Product, the
strongest predictors of a user subscribing
are time spent in the app, time in voice chat, and the number of friends who already have Nitro.
Every product Discord has launched since has built on top of Nitro, rather than attempting to replace it. In 2018, Discord began selling PC games through its own store and shortly afterward allowed developers to
sell games directly through their servers
. It also bundled a game catalog into Nitro, but
removed it a year later
because few subscribers played the titles. The broader sales effort faded as well.
Discord Activities | Source:
Andreessen Horowitz
Discord’s second attempt to court developers came with Activities, which
launched in 2022
as a handful of first-party games playable within voice calls before opening to all developers in 2024. The pitch, prominently
described by Discord investor a16z
, evoked Facebook-era social gaming: instant distribution for casual games across Discord’s social graph. Some games have found audiences: Playroom’s Death by AI reportedly peaked at 700K daily players, ScoreSpace’s Blackjack
claims 1.2M monthly players
, and a licensed version of
Wordle
is also available.
These games share three characteristics: they are short, social, and work well with friends on a call. Activities has yet to produce lasting hits or games with meaningful depth or monetization. Discord also appears to have deprioritized the product, judging by its limited presence in developer marketing materials over the past year. Today, Activities looks less like the next Facebook platform and more like a venue better suited to small studios with limited commercial ambitions. For example,
Distinct Possibility Studios’ five-person team launched a card game
there last month after its AAA shooter failed.
Avatar cosmetics that users can buy in Discord / Source:
TechCrunch
What has stuck is anything that deepens Nitro. The Shop, added in 2023, sells profile cosmetics like avatar decorations and nameplates, with Nitro subscribers as its main customers. Introduced last year,
Orbs
are a currency that users earn by completing sponsored “Quests” and can be spent in the Shop or on short Nitro subscriptions. This May,
Nitro Rewards
bundled in a starter tier of Xbox Game Pass and hardware discounts, with the stated goal of making Nitro “the must-have gaming membership.”
The New Pitch to Game Developers
Discord now offers three new developer-facing products. Most importantly, the
Social SDK
